items.key: TST-0604 The rider marker glides on a short loop (ISS-0317)
items.name: The rider marker glides on a short loop (ISS-0317)
items.text:
Position updates arrive once a second. On a long route a 1 Hz hop is invisible; on a short circuit each update is a large fraction of the visible track, so an unsmoothed marker visibly jumps. That is the defect ISS-0317 fixed and this check guards.

## Setup

- The bundled **Velodrome** route — `route_velodrome`, a **250 m loop**, and it is in the FREE catalogue, so no purchase or import is needed. It is the cheapest way to get the short circuit this check requires; any imported circuit of 1500 m or less also works.
- The **map as the primary view**, not the small inset beside the terrain. Use Route view mode `MAP_ONLY` or the map half of the map-with-terrain-inset layout.
- **Follow mode on**, so the camera tracks the rider.
- A trainer connected and turning, or the mock trainer from Developer Settings — the marker only moves if telemetry is flowing.

## Steps

1. Start the Velodrome route and pedal steadily.
2. Watch the rider marker for two or three laps.

## Expect

- Step 1: the marker moves continuously between updates, covering each second's distance smoothly.
- Step 2: it never sits still and then jumps, and never overshoots the track or lags behind the rider.

## Not this check

- Whether the camera rotates only on real turns — that is [[TST-0605-Heading-Smoothing-ISS-0320]].
- Whether the pulse ring animates around the marker — that is [[TST-0603-Follow-Mode-Pulse-Ring]], and it is excused pending [[ISS-0401-PulseRingIsDrawnButNotSeen]].

## Provenance

Covers [[ISS-0317]].

Split out of [[TST-0013-IosParityAcceptance]] on 2026-08-20. That note was a 107-row iOS parity test; an audit against the acceptance corpus found 63 of its rows already covered and 44 not. This is one of the 44, and it is platform-neutral because the behaviour is unverified on both platforms rather than only on iOS.

Rewritten 2026-09-06 into the Setup / Steps / Expect shape. The previous text asked for "a short circuit of 1500 m or less" without saying that one ships with the app.

items.key: TST-0636 A v2 route ride does not compete with a v1 personal best (ISS-0335)
items.name: A v2 route ride does not compete with a v1 personal best (ISS-0335)
items.text:
On a device carrying route PBs set before 2026-06-18:

## Steps

1. Ride one of those routes again, watching for a ghost.
2. Tap FINISH, then Save ride, and read the celebration's headline.
3. Open the old session in History.

## Expect

- Step 1: no ghost from the old ride appears.
- Step 2: it counts as a first time on the route: `First time on <route>` is the headline or a chip, and nothing says New best on.
- Step 3: the old session still carries its trophy.

## What this guards

This is the `v1` → `v2` physics lineage split. `PhysicsVersion.canonical` went from `v1:cda=0.325;crr=0.005` to `v2:cda=0.36;crr=0.006;…` in ISS-0335, and every ROUTE session stamps the hash of that string at save time (`WorkoutViewModel.kt:2450`, `WorkoutSession.physicsVersion`). `PbCalculator.kt:157` carries it onto each lap attempt, and `PersonalBestDao.getForRiderAndWorkout` matches on it, so a `v2` lap finds no `v1` incumbent and comes back `FIRST`. `GhostRepository` filters candidate laps the same way, which is why the old ghost is gone.

The defect this guards is a stale physics version treated as canonical, which pooled 0.325-era and 0.36-era laps under one hash and compared times that are not comparable. `PhysicsVersionTest` now ties the canonical string to `PhysicsUtils` numerically so the constants and the hash cannot drift apart again.

**One thing to expect that the row previously denied:** the stored `personal_bests` row *is* replaced. Its primary key is `(riderId, workoutProgramId)` with no `physicsVersion` column in it (`PersonalBest.kt:18-21`) and `upsert` is `OnConflictStrategy.REPLACE`, so the `v2` lap writes over the `v1` row. What survives the change is the old session's `wasPbAtTimeOfSave` flag, a historical fact, which is why the trophy stays in History. Only one lineage's PB is live at a time.

**Narrowed 2026-09-12 (TASK-0890).** The row used to open by holding a steady power on a flat route and checking the resulting speed against the calibration figures in TST-0126. TST-0126 runs those figures itself: it carries `command: cd android && ./gradlew :app:testDebugUnitTest --tests com.yourtrainer.utils.PhysicsUtilsTest`, which pins 160 W and 200 W to ±1 km/h. Testing it here bought a second tick on the same assertion and cost a hardware ride. The PB-lineage half had no other cover and is what remains.

*Split out of [[TST-0013-IosParityAcceptance]] on 2026-08-20. That note was a 107-row iOS parity test; an audit against the 579-check acceptance corpus found 63 of its rows already covered by existing checks and 44 not. This is one of the 44. It is written platform-neutral because the behaviour is unverified on both platforms, not only on iOS.*

The results were one part, so the release test could give the whole check only one mark. They are now numbered steps with one expectation each, so a failure in one no longer fails the others (FEAT-0122, criterion A7; [[TASK-0922-CorrectTheWalkCorpus]]). The wording is otherwise unchanged.

## Step 2 reworded 2026-10-10

[[FEAT-0134-WhenARideEndsOneScreenCelebratesItSavesItAndSharesItAsAPicture]] moved the personal-best result from the ride-end summary to the celebration's headline after Save. The claim is unchanged: a v2 ride is a first time, not a comparison with the v1 best.

items.key: TST-0646 A file shared out of Your Trainer keeps its name, and a .ytw comes back in through the importer
items.name: A file shared out of Your Trainer keeps its name, and a .ytw comes back in through the importer
items.text:
[[TST-0642]] proved one file type into one destination. This is the general check behind [[ADR-0013-SharedFileNaming]]: every file the app shares keeps its extension, and the one format the app can re-import round-trips.

## Why a round trip and not just a filename

`WorkoutSelectionScreen.kt:856` refuses a workout import whose display name does not end in a known extension. So a `.ytw` that loses its name in transit cannot come back into Your Trainer — the bug that hit Garmin hits our own importer too, and only a round trip catches it.

## The release test (Android)

Rename a workout to **`Sweet Spot: 2x20`** first. The colon is the whole point: it is the character that caused ISS-0387, and until [[TASK-0806-ShareFileNamingSweep]] it went straight into the `.ytw` filename.

1. Workout library → share that workout → **Save to Drive**. The saved name must be `Sweet_Spot_2x20.ytw` — no colon, extension present.
2. In Your Trainer: import that file back from Drive. It must import as a workout, not bounce off the extension gate with *"supported formats: .ytw or .zwo"*.
3. History → ⋮ → **Export CSV** → Save to Drive. Name must end `.csv`.
4. Settings → **Share Diagnostics** → Save to Drive. Name must end `.txt`.
5. History → ⋮ → **Export FIT** → Save to Drive. Name must end `.fit`. (Overlaps [[TST-0642]]; cheap to do in the same pass.)

## The release test (iOS)

Repeat steps 1, 2 and 5 with the same colon-bearing workout name, per [[TASK-0807-IosExportFileNameSanitisation]]. The saved names must match Android's byte for byte — same sanitiser rules on both platforms, so a divergence here is a parity defect.

Then test steps 3 and 4 through the iOS share sheet. History's CSV export saves as the name the share sheet offers, which must end `.csv`. Settings → About → About Your Trainer → **Share Diagnostics** shares the log; save it to Drive and read the name Drive gives it, which must end `.txt`. Edwin chose the share sheet's names as the iOS evidence on 2026-09-17 ([[ISS-0444-CheckNotesTheV220ProceduresFoundStaleOrUnwalkable]]).

## Expect

- The `.ytw` saves as `Sweet_Spot_2x20.ytw`, with no colon, and imports back as a workout.
- The CSV, diagnostics and FIT names end `.csv`, `.txt` and `.fit`.

## What a failure means

A name arriving without its extension means a receiver read a field the helper does not set, and `ShareIntents.sendFile` needs another one. A name arriving mangled rather than truncated means `safeFileName` is missing a character. Record which destination and which file type; the destination matters as much as the format, since Drive and Gmail disagree about which field they read.

## Not covered here

Whether Garmin Connect accepts the FIT once it has a correct name — that is [[TST-0642]].

items.name: ERG mode at 0 % / gear 9
items.text:
Free Ride, slope-mode = `ERG` (Settings → Hardware), slope = 0 %, gear 9. **Verify target reads ~77 W within ±10 W**, matching the SIM rider effort row above. [1.11]

## Declared automated 2026-09-12 — the number this row exists to check is asserted on every build

`PhysicsUtilsTest` asserts `routeErgTargetPower(0 %, gear 9, LINEAR, FTP 200, 80 kg)` lands in 70..90 W, in the test named `FEAT-0068 — 0pct slope cruise gear matches SIM ~80 W`. That is the same rider, the same corner and the same tolerance the row asks a person to read off the cockpit. Today the function returns 76 W.

The row used to open with "Cockpit shows target wattage", and that sentence was removed here. It is a rendering claim, not an arithmetic one, and [[TST-0037-ERG-Free-Ride-Watts]] already tests it — ERG free ride must show watts rather than a percentage. Nothing leaves the release test that another row was not already asking for.

No status is written here. `tools/scripts/run-tests.py` runs the command and CI is the verdict (ADR-0010 / ADR-0025).

## Also measured on hardware by the gear sweep — 2026-09-12

The `command:` above proves the app computes the right ERG target for this point on every build. It says nothing about whether a trainer *holds* it, which is what a rider used to set this point up to find out.

[[TST-0658-TheGearSweepRidesTheGearTable]] now visits two derived gears at 0 % in ERG mode as part of its cross-mode leg, and records what the rider actually produced beside what was predicted. Test the sweep rather than staging this point on its own.

The predicted figure is a reference the scorecard prints, never a threshold. It comes from one constant fitted to one rider on one trainer (`V_REF_FTP_FRACTION`), and the rider is the actuator. Edwin, 2026-09-12: *"it needs to have some correlation with the original measurements but I don't think we can be very precise?"*

items.key: TST-0643 Exported FIT carries every message the Activity file definition requires (ISS-0387)
items.name: Exported FIT carries every message the Activity file definition requires (ISS-0387)
items.text:
Decodes a file straight out of `FitEncoder` and asserts the global message numbers present include `file_id`, `record`, `lap`, `session` and `activity` — the five the FIT Activity file definition requires. Also asserts the lap's totals match the session's, and that `activity` is the last message in the file.

items.key: TST-0644 Every History filter chip fits and is tappable on a phone (ISS-0390)
items.name: Every History filter chip fits and is tappable on a phone (ISS-0390)
items.text:
**The defect's assertion, and the only claim this row makes:** on a 360 dp phone, all five History filters — All, Power, Route, Heart Rate and PBs — are on screen and readable, and none is clipped off the right edge. ISS-0390 was the trailing **PBs** chip falling outside a 360 dp phone, where it could not be tapped at all.

The case that holds it is `HistoryFiltersSitInHistoryTest.on_a_phone_the_filters_are_under_past_sessions_and_nothing_is_docked_above_the_bar`. It opens History at a pinned 360 dp and asserts that each of the five filters has its label and lies inside the filter row, which fails for a chip pushed off the row's edge. It does not tap the chips on saved rides; those taps are tested by hand in [[TST-0190-Session-Type-Labeling]] and [[TST-0321-History-Trophy-Filter]].

How the filters look is not this row's claim. On Android the chips are a row in History, under the Past Sessions heading (TASK-1068, 2026-10-11). They keep their labels on a phone rather than collapsing to icons; [[TST-0552-Filter-Chips-Render-Dispatch]] carries that. On iOS the chips are still a strip docked to the History destination until TASK-1066, and this command does not run there.

**The width is pinned, not taken from the device.** A check that relied on the device's own width would pass on a tablet with the defect present, which is how this shipped. Pinning 360 dp makes the guard independent of whatever hardware runs it.

## History of this row

Until 2026-09-22 the command ran `HistoryTypeFilterRowTest`, nine cases over the in-page `HistoryTypeFilterRow`. The one that pinned the defect was `all_five_chips_fit_within_a_small_phone_width`, a geometry check on the PBs chip's right edge; two more pinned the icon-only collapse under 600 dp, which the new strip no longer does. That class was deleted with the in-page row. The earlier fix had turned `assertExists` into `assertIsDisplayed` and a synthetic `OnClick` into a real `performClick`; the new case keeps the first. Verified 2026-09-02 on an SM-X910 under the old class.

From 2026-09-22 to 2026-10-11 the command ran `NavigationContainerTest`, whose case `history_filters_keep_their_labels_on_a_360dp_phone` laid the docked strip out at 360 dp. TASK-1068 moved the filters into History and deleted that case with the strip.

items.key: TST-0645 A PRO rider can import their own history, and it lands on the rider they can see (ISS-0392)
items.name: A PRO rider can import their own history, and it lands on the rider they can see (ISS-0392)
items.text:
Fifteen unit cases over `RiderImportPlanner`, plus three instrumentation cases that cover the wiring a pure function cannot.

**The case that pins the defect is `PRO with an unmatched name lands on the seat instead of the add path that always fails`.** Before the fix, a file whose profile name did not exactly match the rider's produced `ImportConflict.None`, whose dialog offers only "add as a new rider" — and `Tier.riderCap(PRO)` is 1, so that action was refused every time. The rider could not import their own history at all.

**The guard against the second defect is `a name match on a hidden rider never reaches the dialog`** and its overlap twin. Both detection queries read the whole rider table, so under PRO the dialog could name a rider the tier does not show, and merging landed the data back out of sight — ISS-0386's symptom arriving through the door ISS-0386 declared safe.

`no outcome under PRO with riders can ever be the add path` sweeps the reachable inputs rather than asserting one of them. That is the invariant the fix actually establishes, and asserting it directly is what stops a later branch quietly re-opening the dead end.

The FREE and FAMILY cases are not padding. The change filters detection through `LicenseSeatResolver.visibleRiders`, which returns every rider off PRO — so those cases are what prove the filter is a no-op where it should be, and that the four existing dialogs still reach their existing outcomes.

**Red-then-green, verified 2026-09-04.** Both defects were re-introduced into `RiderImportPlanner` — the PRO stage deleted and the two visibility filters removed — and 7 of the 15 unit cases failed. The 8 FREE/FAMILY cases stayed green throughout, which is the evidence they are not over-constrained. Restored, all 15 pass.

Instrumentation verified 2026-09-04 on an SM-X910 (Android 16): 48 tests in `com.yourtrainer.data.backup`, all green. That run includes `merge_keeps_the_target_riders_profile_and_never_takes_the_files`, which pins Edwin's second decision — the target rider's FTP, weight, max HR and LTHR survive an import that carries different ones.

**Not covered here:** the rider-facing half. Whether the confirmation copy actually tells a rider where their rides are going is a judgement about understanding, not something these assert. That belongs with the FEAT-0104 acceptance rows.

items.key: TST-0660 Each preset counts its own gears — 26 for Linear, 22 for Road, 12 for MTB — and a rider who never chose one gets Linear
items.name: Each preset counts its own gears — 26 for Linear, 22 for Road, 12 for MTB — and a rider who never chose one gets Linear
items.text:
The number a rider reads in the cockpit's `GEAR N of M` label, and the number printed on each chip in Profile → Preferences, both come from `VirtualGearTables.gearCount(preset)`. This check asserts that function returns 26 for LINEAR, 22 for ROAD_COMPACT and 12 for MTB_1X, and that the resistance and grade tables behind each preset hold that many entries.

`VirtualGearTablesTest` asserts it in `linear_has_26_gears`, `road_compact_has_22_gears` and `mtb_1x_has_12_gears`. Each of the three checks the count function and both tables together, so a table edited without its count, or a count changed without its table, fails the build.

The same class also asserts that a rider who never picked a preset still gets Linear. `fromString_null_resolves_to_LINEAR` and `fromString_unknown_resolves_to_LINEAR` cover the stored-preference path, and `resistanceForGear_default_arg_returns_LINEAR` and `gradeForGear_default_arg_returns_LINEAR` walk all 26 gears to show that a call site which passes no preset produces LINEAR values unchanged.

## Why this note exists separately

Three acceptance rows made this arithmetic claim inside a larger claim a rider has to test. Splitting the arithmetic out lets each of those rows keep `automation: manual` and stay in the release gate for the half a person still performs, which a `command:` on the original row would have silently removed (`tools/instructions/TESTING.md` § "Release gating"). The three rows are [[TST-0036-Simulation-Gear-Shifting]] (the buttons sit below the slope controls and the label renders), [[TST-0118-Gear-Shifting]] (the buttons appear in simulation mode and a shift is felt) and [[TST-0127-Virtual-Gear-Presets-Picker-Visibility-TASK]] (the three chips render in Profile → Preferences and an existing rider defaults to Linear).

No status is written here. `tools/scripts/run-tests.py` runs the command and CI is the verdict (ADR-0010 / ADR-0025).

items.key: TST-0661 Shifting up never gets easier, and every preset's table ends where its preset says it does
items.name: Shifting up never gets easier, and every preset's table ends where its preset says it does
items.text:
On all three presets, resistance must never fall as the gear number rises, and the grade offset must never fall either. `VirtualGearTablesTest` asserts both across every entry of every table, in `all_resistance_tables_are_non_decreasing` and `all_grade_tables_are_non_decreasing`.

**Non-decreasing, not strictly increasing, and that is deliberate.** `ROAD_COMPACT_RESISTANCE` holds 45 at both gear 13 and gear 14. That pair is a real 2×11 cassette overlap where two adjacent chainring-and-cog combinations resolve to the same ratio, and the test's comment names it. A rider shifting 13 → 14 on Road feels nothing change, by design. LINEAR is the preset where every shift does change resistance, and [[TST-0425-No-Dead-Gears]] is the row that asks a person to feel it.

The endpoints are asserted in the same class. `all_resistance_tables_anchor_to_5_at_bottom` puts every preset's gear 1 at 5 %, the shared warm-up floor. `resistance_top_anchors_per_preset` puts LINEAR's top gear at 82 % and both cassette presets at 72 %. `all_grade_tables_anchor_to_neg3_at_bottom` and `all_grade_tables_anchor_to_pos3_at_top` hold every preset's grade band at −3.00 to +3.00, which is what keeps the slope extremes feeling the same whichever preset a rider picks.

One more assertion belongs to the same claim: `resistanceForGear_returns_different_values_for_different_presets` compares gear 6 across the three tables and fails if two of them agree. The regression it guards is Road or MTB silently resolving to the LINEAR table, which would make the preset picker decorative.

## Why this note exists separately

The three rows that made this claim each also ask a rider for something a machine cannot supply, so they keep `automation: manual` and stay in the release gate: [[TST-0118-Gear-Shifting]] (a shift is felt in simulation mode), [[TST-0130-Virtual-Gear-Presets-ROAD-COMPACT-Cassette]] (the low gears step further apart than the high ones) and [[TST-0131-Virtual-Gear-Presets-MTB-1X-Wider]] (gear 1 light, gear 12 heavy, and the cockpit buttons clamping at the ends).

No status is written here. `tools/scripts/run-tests.py` runs the command and CI is the verdict (ADR-0010 / ADR-0025).

items.key: TST-0662 Every preset starts the rider on its own cruise gear, and all three land near the same 30 % effort
items.name: Every preset starts the rider on its own cruise gear, and all three land near the same 30 % effort
items.text:
Switching preset resets the rider to that preset's cruise gear rather than carrying the old gear number across. A gear number means a different effort in each table, so carrying it over would change the rider's effort silently. `VirtualGearTables.defaultGear(preset)` is the function that decides, and it returns 9 for LINEAR, 7 for ROAD_COMPACT and 5 for MTB_1X.

`VirtualGearTablesTest` asserts LINEAR exactly: `linear_default_gear_is_9` checks both that the function returns 9 and that `LINEAR_RESISTANCE[8]` is 30 %, which is the historical cruise feel TASK-0459 had to preserve when it moved that feel from gear 10 of 22 to gear 9 of 26.

The two cassette presets are asserted as effort rather than as a gear number. `road_compact_default_gear_resists_close_to_30pct` requires the default gear's resistance to sit in 25..35 %, and `mtb_1x_default_gear_resists_close_to_30pct` requires 25..40 % — a wider window because MTB steps are bigger and no gear hits 30 % exactly. Today those resolve to gear 7 at 31 % and gear 5 at 35 %.

**The gap this note used to name is closed.** The two cassette assertions pinned the *effort*, not the *gear number*, so a re-tune that moved ROAD_COMPACT's cruise gear from 7 to 8 while keeping it inside 25..35 % would have passed while the cockpit read `GEAR 8 of 22`. `every_preset_starts_on_the_cruise_gear_the_cockpit_prints` now asserts 9, 7 and 5 as numbers, and `every_preset_cruise_gear_is_inside_its_own_table` checks each one falls inside its own table ([[TASK-0888-AssertTheTwoNarrowedGearClaims]]).

What still needs a person is the screen, not the number: [[TST-0132-Virtual-Gear-Presets-Preset-Switch-Resets]] asks someone to navigate Profile → Preferences and read `GEAR 7 of 22` and `GEAR 5 of 12` off the cockpit. A test can prove the function returns 7; only a rider can prove the label shows it.

## Why this note exists separately

Three rows made this claim alongside something a rider has to do: [[TST-0132-Virtual-Gear-Presets-Preset-Switch-Resets]] (navigate Profile → Preferences and back, and read the cockpit label), [[TST-0130-Virtual-Gear-Presets-ROAD-COMPACT-Cassette]] and [[TST-0131-Virtual-Gear-Presets-MTB-1X-Wider]] (the feel of the steps). All three keep `automation: manual` so their remainders stay in the release gate.

No status is written here. `tools/scripts/run-tests.py` runs the command and CI is the verdict (ADR-0010 / ADR-0025).

items.key: TST-0663 Slope and gear each move resistance on their own — the slope adds half its value on top of whatever the gear already asks for
items.name: Slope and gear each move resistance on their own — the slope adds half its value on top of whatever the gear already asks for
items.text:
Setting a slope does not replace the gear's contribution, it adds to it. `PhysicsUtils.effectiveGrade` halves the rider's slope — the Zwift-style 50 % trainer-difficulty scaling — and adds the gear's own grade offset on top.

`PhysicsUtilsLinearSnapshotTest` asserts the addition at three slopes. `effectiveGrade_flat_road_returns_pure_gear_offset` shows that at 0 % the result collapses to the gear offset alone: −3.00 at gear 1, −0.12 at gear 13, 3.00 at gear 26. `effectiveGrade_5pct_slope_adds_2_5pct_to_each_gear` shows the same three gears moving to −0.50, 2.38 and 5.50, each exactly 2.5 higher. `effectiveGrade_10pct_slope_adds_5pct_to_each_gear` and `effectiveGrade_negative_slope_descends` repeat it at 10 % and at −5 %.

The dispatched level follows. `simulationResistance_flat_road_75kg_rider` gives 5, 31 and 63 at gears 1, 11 and 26 on the flat; `simulationResistance_5pct_slope_75kg_rider` gives 32, 55 and 80 at the same three gears on a 5 % climb. Read across, the slope moved every gear; read down, the gear still moves the level while the slope is held. That pair is the row's claim that the two controls act independently.

## Why this note exists separately

[[TST-0120-Slope-Gears]] made this claim and also carries an `invalidated_by` from TASK-0460: the Free Ride cockpit's slope Row moved inside a Column, and someone has to confirm the tap targets still work and the gear Row still sits beneath as a sibling. That is a layout check, so TST-0120 keeps `automation: manual` and stays in the release gate for it.

[[TST-0430-Slope-Gears-Together]] makes the same arithmetic claim under [[ISS-0130]] and carries no layout remainder, so it took this command directly and reads `automation: full`. The two notes run the same class on purpose: one records the claim for the feature, the other records it for the defect, and they are cross-linked so a future edit to either finds the other.

No status is written here. `tools/scripts/run-tests.py` runs the command and CI is the verdict (ADR-0010 / ADR-0025).

items.key: TST-0664 The trainer is never told to free-spin — gear 1 on the flat and a steep descent both floor at level 5
items.name: The trainer is never told to free-spin — gear 1 on the flat and a steep descent both floor at level 5
items.text:
SIM physics says a rider in the lowest gear on flat or falling ground needs 0 W, and 0 % dispatched to the trainer feels like a dropped chain on some hardware. `PhysicsUtils.simulationResistance` therefore coerces its output to a 5 % floor, and this check asserts the floor holds at both edges.

`PhysicsUtilsLinearSnapshotTest` asserts the flat edge in `simulationResistance_flat_road_75kg_rider`: gear 1 at 0 % returns 5, and the same call for a 95 kg rider also returns 5, so the floor is not an accident of one rider weight. It asserts the descent edge in `simulationResistance_descent_floors_at_5pct_level`: gear 1 at −15 % returns 5.

**Widened 2026-09-12, and one claim corrected.** The descent assertion covered a single point, gear 1 at −15 %. `simulationResistance_descent_floors_in_the_gears_TST_0157_samples` now adds gear 9 at −3 % and gear 13 at −5 %, at two rider weights each — the gears [[TST-0157-Resistance-Edge-Descent-Floors-At-5]] asks a rider to sample.

`TST-0157` used to claim the floor held for *any* gear at or below −3 %. It does not, and should not: a high gear trims the grade upward, so gear 26 on a −3 % descent arrives as +1.5 % and is a climb. `simulationResistance_does_not_floor_a_high_gear_on_a_shallow_descent` pins that boundary so the floor is not later "completed" to swallow it. See [[TASK-0888-AssertTheTwoNarrowedGearClaims]].

## Why this note exists separately

Two rows made this claim and each also asks for something only a rider on a trainer can report. [[TST-0156-Resistance-Edge-Gear-1-0-Floors]] asks whether the floor feels like a very light spin rather than a dropped chain, and [[TST-0157-Resistance-Edge-Descent-Floors-At-5]] asks whether the trainer stays out of genuine free-spin on the road. Both keep `automation: manual` so those remainders stay in the release gate.

No status is written here. `tools/scripts/run-tests.py` runs the command and CI is the verdict (ADR-0010 / ADR-0025).

items.key: TST-0665 Top gear on a 5 % climb dispatches level 80, leaving headroom — only an impossible climb saturates at 100
items.name: Top gear on a 5 % climb dispatches level 80, leaving headroom — only an impossible climb saturates at 100
items.text:
The hardest gear on a 5 % climb has to stay below the trainer's ceiling, otherwise there is nothing left for a steeper climb and every hard effort feels identical. `PhysicsUtilsLinearSnapshotTest` asserts the number in `simulationResistance_5pct_slope_75kg_rider`: gear 26 at 5 % for a 75 kg rider dispatches level 80, which is both the "~80 %" figure the acceptance row quotes and its "does not saturate at 100 %" claim.

The ceiling is asserted too, so the headroom is a real gap rather than a missing clamp. `simulationResistance_steep_climb_caps_at_100` puts a 95 kg rider in gear 26 on a 20 % climb and gets 100. `simulationResistance_10pct_slope_75kg_rider` fills in the middle at 56, 73 and 95 for gears 1, 11 and 26.

## Why this note exists separately

[[TST-0158-Resistance-Edge-Gear-26-5-Near]] also claims the rider's own effort there lands around 530 W, roughly 2.5 × FTP for the reference rider, and no unit test can assert what a person produced. That row keeps `automation: manual`. It is also a one-off rather than something [[TST-0658]] absorbs: gear 26 sits above the gear sweep's derived ceiling, so the sweep never rides it.

No status is written here. `tools/scripts/run-tests.py` runs the command and CI is the verdict (ADR-0010 / ADR-0025).

items.key: TST-0430 Slope + Gears Together
items.name: Slope + Gears Together
items.text:
In simulation mode, set slope to 5% and shift gears. Verify both controls independently affect resistance — slope sets the hill, gears adjust effort within it.

## Declared automated 2026-09-12 — both halves of the claim are asserted on every build

`PhysicsUtilsLinearSnapshotTest` asserts each half separately. `effectiveGrade_5pct_slope_adds_2_5pct_to_each_gear` shows the slope adding a flat 2.5 % on top of whatever grade offset the gear carries: gear 1 moves from −3.00 to −0.50, gear 13 from −0.12 to 2.38, gear 26 from 3.00 to 5.50. `simulationResistance_5pct_slope_75kg_rider` shows the gear still moving the dispatched level while that slope is held: 32, 55 and 80 at gears 1, 11 and 26. Set beside `simulationResistance_flat_road_75kg_rider` (5, 31, 63 at the same gears) the pair is exactly the row's claim — each control moves resistance on its own.

This row carries no cockpit or layout claim and no `invalidated_by`, so nothing is left for a rider once the arithmetic is machine-checked. The sibling row [[TST-0120-Slope-Gears]] makes the same arithmetic claim and does carry a layout remainder, so it stays manual and its arithmetic half is [[TST-0663]].

No status is written here. `tools/scripts/run-tests.py` runs the command and CI is the verdict (ADR-0010 / ADR-0025).

items.key: TST-0452 First-Transition Reset
items.name: First-Transition Reset
items.text:
An HR-Zone workout whose first interval is shorter than 60 seconds opens its lookahead window before the ride starts. The controller must hand over to the next zone on that first transition without stalling: the effective target zone is already the *next* zone at tick 0, so the flip never happens at a boundary the rider can see. `HrZoneLookahead` clamps the lead to half the interval for exactly this case, and the controller's status machine picks up the new target on the next `tick()`.

## The observation method this row had is gone; the assertion is not

The row used to say "watch the `auto · converging` status banner at tick 0 vs. tick 1". That banner does not render. ISS-0166 and ISS-0167 replaced it with the delta pill and the heartbeat progress bar under the watts row (`ActiveWorkoutScreen.kt:1680-1690`), and `hrZoneAlgorithmStatus` now drives only one visible thing: the watts number greys out when the HRM is lost (`ActiveWorkoutScreen.kt:1725`). There is no tick-0-vs-tick-1 status text to read off the screen any more.

The reset itself also moved. `WorkoutViewModel.kt:1734-1740` records the decision: an effective-zone change no longer resets the controller, because resetting there restarted the rate window and cost up to 20 seconds of dead time in the middle of the pre-ramp. The controller's `tick()` just receives the new `targetZone` and its status machine recovers on its own.

What is left is arithmetic and a state machine, and both run under unit test. `HrZoneLookaheadTest` pins the lookahead-already-open case (`short interval clamps lead to half the duration`, `very short interval still pre-ramps in its second half`); `HrZoneLockControllerTest` pins the status machine and `reset()`. The `command:` below runs both classes and was verified to run.

No status is stamped here — that belongs to `tools/scripts/run-tests.py`, from an exit code, never to a hand (ADR-0010).

items.key: TST-0488 Mid-ride preference change — non-SIM trainer
items.name: Mid-ride preference change — non-SIM trainer
items.text:
Start a Route ride on a non-SIM trainer with `Auto` → cockpit shows `· ERG (auto)`. Change Slope behaviour to `Resistance` while the ride is running. Since PHASE-025 (2026-09-22) the cockpit has no route to Settings, so a rider can no longer make this change by hand mid-ride; the automated test below drives the same flag change directly. The combined `supportsSimParams + slopeMode` flow in `MainActivity` should propagate the change without requiring a ride restart. *(automated: `WorkoutViewModelDispatchTest.onSimParamsChanged_*` — flag math covered; BLE response stays hardware-dependent.)*

items.key: TST-0544 Ride-mode strip — docked to Workouts, one mode selected, tap dispatch
items.name: Ride-mode strip — docked to Workouts, one mode selected, tap dispatch
items.text:
— `NavigationContainerTest`. The Power / Route / Heart Rate tabs that sat in the Workouts content (`WorkoutTypeTabs`) were deleted on 2026-09-22, with their test; the ride modes are now one control attached to the Workouts destination (FEAT-0124). On Android it is docked above the bottom bar on a phone and lies across the top of Workouts on a tablet (TASK-1069, 2026-10-11). The cases that carry this row: `ride_modes_dock_above_the_bar_with_exactly_one_selected` (on a phone the strip sits directly above the bottom bar, exactly one mode is selected, and tapping Route dispatches `WorkoutType.ROUTE`), `in_the_rail_nothing_nests_under_workouts` (on a tablet the rail nests no modes under Workouts), `settings_has_no_children_and_no_strip`, and the two reduced-motion cases. The command runs the whole class, so its other cases, the bar and the rail, run with it. This command does not run the unit tests for the tablet's bar and the sliding highlight: `RideModeListSlideTest.on_a_tablet_the_modes_lie_across_the_top_of_workouts` and `RideModeTrackTest`. On iOS the three modes still nest under Workouts in the rail until TASK-1066.

items.name: The debug-workout toggle hides and shows the [Debug] workouts
items.text:
One toggle, flipped once, with the library checked either side of it.

On iOS, open Settings → About and tap Version three times to reveal the inline Developer · Workouts section. Its Show debug workouts toggle is the control for these two observations. On Android, use the Developer Settings screen.

## Procedure

1. **Off — hidden.** With "Show debug workouts" off in Developer Settings, no workout with the `[Debug]` prefix appears anywhere in the library.
2. **On — visible.** Turn "Show debug workouts" on. The debug workouts appear.

*(Partially automated: `WorkoutRepositoryLibraryTest` exercises the `isDevShowTestWorkouts()` gating on both sides. The Developer Settings toggle itself stays manual.)*

## Expected results

- Step 1: with the toggle off, no workout with the `[Debug]` prefix appears anywhere in the library.
- Step 2: with the toggle on, the debug workouts appear.

## Rows this row absorbed — 2026-09-12

| Retired | What it asked for | Taken at |
| --- | --- | --- |
| [[TST-0097-Debug-Workouts-Visible]] | debug workouts appear once the toggle is on | step 2 |

## What one tick no longer distinguishes

- **TST-0097** — a toggle stuck in one position fails this row whichever position it is stuck in, and shipping debug workouts to riders is the worse of the two failures.

## Evidence (fill after running)

- What the library showed with the toggle off and on.

items.name: Seven taps opens Developer Settings, and Debug Workouts is inside it
items.text:

## Procedure

1. **Seven taps.** On the About category body, tap the `Version X.Y.Z` text seven times. Developer Settings opens.
2. **Debug Workouts is there.** In Developer Settings, the "Debug Workouts" section is present, with its toggle switch.

## On iOS

2. **Show debug workouts is there.** Among them, the **Developer · Workouts** section carries the "Show debug workouts" toggle.

## Expected results

- [android] Step 1: seven taps open Developer Settings.
- [ios] Step 1: three taps show the Developer sections in Settings.
- Step 2: the debug-workout toggle is there.

## Rows this row absorbed — 2026-09-12

| Retired | What it asked for | Taken at |
| --- | --- | --- |
| [[TST-0113-Developer-Options]] | the Debug Workouts section and its toggle exist in Developer Settings | step 2 |

## What one tick no longer distinguishes

items.name: Gear Power Range (LINEAR 26-gear retune)
items.text:
## Steps

At 80 rpm on flat (0 %) with the LINEAR preset, ride gears 1, 9, 18 and 26. Pre-TASK-0459 figures (gear 5 ≈ 135 W, gear 22 ≈ 380 W) no longer apply.

## Expect

- The watt steps between gears 1, 9, 18 and 26 feel even.

## Original wording

At 80 RPM on flat (0 % slope) with the default LINEAR preset, ride gear 1, gear 9, gear 18 and gear 26 and judge whether the watt deltas feel evenly stepped. Pre-TASK-0459 figures (gear 5 ≈ 135 W, gear 22 ≈ 380 W) no longer apply.

## Narrowed 2026-09-12 — the four resistances are already frozen, and the even-step judgement is the sweep's

The percentages this row used to spot-check — 5 %, 30 %, 57 % and 82 % at gears 1, 9, 18 and 26 — are not sampled by hand any more. `resistanceForGear_each_step_matches_baseline_table` in `PhysicsUtilsLinearSnapshotTest` freezes all 26 LINEAR values on every build, and [[TST-0129-Virtual-Gear-Presets-LINEAR-Retuned-Baseline]] is the acceptance row that carries that command.

What is left is the judgement the numbers cannot make: whether the watts a rider produces step evenly from gear to gear. [[TST-0658]] measures exactly that. Its step 6 reports the delta between adjacent gears across the climb and flags a gear that jumps twice as far as its neighbours, which is the finding this row was asking a rider to feel. Run the sweep and read its scorecard rather than sampling four gears by hand; this row stays in the release test as the place that records the judgement.

items.name: The gear sweep climbs the real gear table, stops where it said it would, and its watts rise with every gear
items.text:
This is the release test that proves the tool measures the gears rather than the trainer. It replaces the measurement half of a dozen rows. `TST-0143` to `TST-0155` each ask for one reading on the trainer, and this check takes all of them in one run.

## Setup

A trainer that accepts control, such as the KICKR.

The **LINEAR** gear preset. The sweep refuses any other preset rather than switching the rider's setting.

A rider able to hold about 80 rpm from gear 1 up to whatever ceiling the tool derives. The numbers below assume the reference rider: **200 W FTP and 80 kg**. Check the rider's FTP and weight in Profile before starting.

Developer Options: "Run gear sweep". For step 10, tick "Run this test against a mock trainer (no hardware; ~15 s, not remembered)", set "Failure mode:" to "Refuses control", and the button becomes "Run gear sweep against mock".

## Steps

1. **Where the sweep lives.** Open Developer Options and find "Run gear sweep" beside "Run trainer compatibility test". Then open Settings → Hardware → Trainer compatibility as an ordinary rider would, and look for it there.
2. **The ceiling.** Start the sweep. Before the first gear is set, read the top gear it will climb to and the watts it predicts there.
3. **Overruling the ceiling.** Lower the top gear by one, then raise it by one, then set it back.
4. **The climb.** Pedal steadily at about 80 rpm and let it run from gear 1 to the ceiling. Watch the gear number change on screen at each step.
5. **The watts.** Read the scorecard's average watts for each gear.
6. **The deltas.** Read the step between adjacent gears across the climb.
7. **The corners, in all three modes.** Let the run continue into the corner leg: two gears at 0 % and two at 5 %, each in SIM, then ERG, then Resistance. That is twelve readings.
8. **The Resistance anchors.** Read the corner leg's Resistance passes at 0 %.
9. **The three modes agree.** Read the spread between SIM, ERG and Resistance at each corner, and the median measured-over-predicted ratio.
10. **A trainer the app cannot drive.** Tick "Run this test against a mock trainer (no hardware; ~15 s, not remembered)", set "Failure mode:" to "Refuses control", and tap "Run gear sweep against mock".
11. **The scorecard.** Look for any way to send the scorecard anywhere.

## Expect

- [android] Step 1: "Run gear sweep" is in Developer Options, and there is no gear sweep in Settings → Hardware → Trainer compatibility.
- [ios] Step 1: "Run gear sweep" is in Settings → Developer · Trainer, and not in Settings → Equipment → Check Trainer Compatibility.
- Step 2: before anything moves, it names the top gear and predicted watts: gear 15, about 179 W, for the reference rider.
- Step 3: the prediction updates with each change.
- Step 4: the gear number changes on screen at each step.
- Step 5: average watts rise gear to gear, none flagged dead. Gear 9 near 80 W, gear 15 near 180 W, for the reference rider.
- Step 6: the step between adjacent gears is roughly constant. No gear jumps twice as far as its neighbours.
- Step 7: for the reference rider the corners are gears 7 and 15 at 0 %, and gears 2 and 4 at 5 %.
- Step 8: the Resistance watts sit near the SIM figures for the same gears.
- Step 9: spread within about 15 % at each corner; over 20 % reads "evidence for a per-rider trainer-feel multiplier", not FAIL. The printed median ratio is that multiplier.
- Step 10: the sweep declines to run and says why. It does not report twenty-six dead gears.
- Step 11: there is no way to submit the scorecard, and running it changes nothing about the compatibility test's Pro grant.

## Not this check

- Stopping mid-sweep because the rider cannot hold cadence: [[TST-0659-TheSweepStopsWhenTheRiderCannotHoldCadence]].
- The six 5 % rows in gears 9 and 15 (`TST-0145`, `TST-0146`, `TST-0149`, `TST-0150`, `TST-0153`, `TST-0154`). The effort cap keeps the sweep out of that region, so they remain separate rides.
- The gears above the ceiling. Their arithmetic is frozen by `PhysicsUtilsLinearSnapshotTest`, which pins all 26 LINEAR values. `TST-0427` is the separate subjective row for the top of the table.
- The trainer compatibility test, which writes targets straight at the trainer and never consults the gear table.

## Evidence (fill after running)

- The scorecard for the run: watts per gear, deltas, and the four corners in three modes.
- The rider's FTP and weight at the time, so the ceiling and the expected watts can be derived again later.

## Notes

- Step 1 is not optional. It is the check that keeps the tool outside the Android feature freeze.
- Step 3: a rider who knows they are having a bad day can stop the tool climbing into it.
- Step 5 discharges [[TST-0143]] and [[TST-0144]]. On a trainer that supports SIM, the climb sets each gear as a SIM grade, which is the dispatch those two rows were written for.
- Step 6: a gear that jumps twice as far as its neighbours is the finding `TST-0119` was asking a rider to feel.
- Step 7: the corner gears are derived, not fixed. The 5 % gears are low on purpose: at gear 9 that slope asks 255 W, and at gear 15 it asks 358 W. The tool will not ask a rider to hold that.
- Step 8: the trainer holding a level should cost the rider about what the same gear cost under SIM. This step discharges [[TST-0151]] and [[TST-0152]].
- Step 9 discharges [[TST-0155]].
- `TST-0427`'s stated wattage is stale; see [[TASK-0882-DeclareTheGearRowsCiAlreadyRuns]].

## Rows this test absorbed — 2026-09-12

Five checks were retired into this one under [[TASK-0889-MergeTheCoveredCalibrationRowsIntoTheSweep]]. Each asked for one reading that a leg of this sweep now takes, and each is named at the step that takes it.

| Retired | What it asked for | Discharged at |
| --- | --- | --- |
| [[TST-0143]] | SIM, 0 %, gear 9, about 80 W | step 5 |
| [[TST-0144]] | SIM, 0 %, gear 15, about 180 W | step 5 |
| [[TST-0151]] | Resistance, 0 %, gear 9, matching SIM | step 8 |
| [[TST-0152]] | Resistance, 0 %, gear 15, matching SIM | step 8 |
| [[TST-0155]] | the three modes within about 15 % at a corner | step 9 |

**What the merge costs.** Five ticks became one. A sweep that goes right at gear 9 and wrong at gear 15 now records as one failure, rather than against the row for that gear. The scorecard prints per-gear numbers, so the detail survives for a reader even though the ledger holds one verdict.

## On iOS, added 2026-09-24

The iOS gear sweep exists since [[TASK-0925-IosDebugControlsForTheOwedChecks]] (2026-09-17). Show the developer sections by tapping the Version row in Settings → About three times; "Run gear sweep" is in Developer · Trainer. The Linear preset is in the Profile section of Settings. The top gear is changed with a stepper before `Start sweep`.

Step 10 on iOS: the iOS sweep has no mock checkbox of its own. Turn on Use mock trainer in Developer · Trainer, set Mock trainer capability to Data-only and Mock failure mode to None, fully close and reopen the app, and reconnect the mock trainer. Then open Run gear sweep: it declines before the first gear and says the trainer's resistance is set by hand. Turn Use mock trainer off, set Mock trainer capability back to Off and restart before the next ride on the KICKR.

items.name: Stopping pedalling mid-sweep ends the run, backs the trainer off, and marks nothing as failed
items.text:
Edwin raised the concern this check exists for, on 2026-09-12: *"I am a little concerned about the higher gears, I don't think I will be able to keep the cadence."* The derived ceiling is the prediction. This check is what happens when the prediction is wrong.

The single most important line: **an early stop is never a FAIL.** A rider who runs out of legs in gear 12 has not found a defect in gear 13.

## Setup

A trainer that accepts control, such as the KICKR, and the LINEAR gear preset.

**Test it after [[TST-0658-TheGearSweepRidesTheGearTable]] has passed.** Deliberately stopping mid-sweep is the whole procedure, so the sweep must already be known to work. The `after:` field says the same thing to the generator, which prints this check second.

Developer Options: "Run gear sweep".

## Steps

1. Start a gear sweep and let it climb normally through the first few gears, so there are real recorded watts to check afterwards.
2. Around gear 10 or 11, drop below 60 rpm for a second or two, then pick the cadence back up.
3. Now stop pedalling, or drop to a slow turn clearly under 60 rpm, and hold that.
4. Put a foot back on the pedal and feel the resistance.
5. Read the top of the scorecard as a stranger would.
6. Read the rows for the gears already ridden.
7. Read every row for a gear not reached, including the corner leg if the stop came before it.
8. Look for a dead-gear flag on every row.

## Expect

- Step 1: the sweep climbs normally through the first few gears.
- Step 2: the sweep keeps going. A dropped notification or a slow stroke at a shift must not end a run.
- Step 3: after about five seconds under 60 rpm, the sweep ends on its own.
- Step 4: the trainer has backed off to gear 9, the cruise gear, not the gear the sweep stopped in.
- Step 5: the top of the scorecard names the stop gear, with cadence as the reason. It reads neither as a crash nor as rider error.
- Step 6: gears 1 up to the stop keep their recorded watts and deltas.
- Step 7: gears not reached read `NOT_RUN`, shown as a dash, not as `FAIL`.
- Step 8: the dead-gear flag appears only on gears actually ridden, and nothing anywhere in the output reads `FAIL`.

## Not this check

- Whether the sweep's watts, ceiling and corners are right: [[TST-0658-TheGearSweepRidesTheGearTable]].
- The compatibility test's abort scorecard, whose shape this one borrows: [[TST-0010-CompatTestAbortScorecard]].

## Evidence (fill after running)

- The scorecard from the interrupted run, showing the ridden gears, the `NOT_RUN` rows and the stop reason.

## Notes

60 rpm is not a threshold invented for this check. It is already the line for a valid sample in the compatibility harness: `PowerAtCadenceStats.validSamples` counts samples at 60 rpm and above. Below it, the watts are not comparable to the watts above it, so carrying on would record numbers the scorecard could not use.

The abort scorecard shape comes from [[TST-0010-CompatTestAbortScorecard]]. `TASK-0591` found that a scorecard full of dashes with no explanation reads as a crash, which is why step 5 checks the explanation and not just the rows.

## On iOS, added 2026-09-24

The iOS gear sweep exists since [[TASK-0925-IosDebugControlsForTheOwedChecks]] (2026-09-17): tap the Version row in Settings → About three times, then Developer · Trainer → Run gear sweep. The rest of the check reads the same on iOS.

items.name: Empty History
items.text:
Open workout history for a rider with zero completed sessions.

## Steps

1. **The empty-state copy.** Read the History screen.
2. **No shimmer.** Look at where the session cards would be.

## Expect

- Step 1: "No workouts yet — complete a ride to see your history here." is shown.
- Step 2: no shimmer loading cards persist, and no blank cards are shown in their place.

## What is automated

*(partially automated: `WorkoutHistoryViewModelTest` exercises the empty-session state through the VM; the exact copy and the shimmer visibility stay manual.)*

## Absorbed 2026-09-12 — what one tick no longer distinguishes

This row absorbed [[TST-0436]], which was the same check written twice. TST-0436 carried the exact copy string and this row did not, so its wording is what survives above; `[[FEAT-0060]]` moved onto this row's `covers:` so nothing loses its coverage.

One tick no longer separates wrong copy from a shimmer that never stops. The second was the defect this check was created for, so say which of the two you saw.

## Numbered 2026-09-17

The results were a numbered list with no `## Steps` heading, so the release test read them as one part and could give the whole check only one mark. They now sit under `## Steps`, with one expectation each under `## Expect`, so a failure in one no longer fails the others (FEAT-0122, criterion A7; [[TASK-0922-CorrectTheWalkCorpus]]). The wording is otherwise unchanged.

items.text:
Complete a workout to land on the History screen.

## Steps

2. From History, tap the rider's name in the bottom bar or rail, then press Back from History.

## Expect

- [android] Step 2: the riders page opens, with no **Switch rider** or **Profile** by the bar or rail. Back from History lands there too.
- [ios] Step 2: the rider item opens Riders with **Switch rider** selected. Back from History lands there too.

## Background

(TASK-0395 / ISS-0180 — the navigate+launchSingleTop combination silently no-op'd when workout_selection was already on the back stack; replaced with `popBackStack` for the back-direction peer-swap.)

## Numbered 2026-09-17

They are now numbered steps with one expectation each, so a failure in one no longer fails the others (FEAT-0122, criterion A7; [[TASK-0922-CorrectTheWalkCorpus]]). items.name: Analytics
items.text:
Complete a 5-minute workout. Verify the session appears in "History" with correct Avg/Max stats and a rendered Power/HR graph. *(partially automated: `WorkoutSessionRepositoryTest` + `MetricRepositoryTest` + `AnalyticsMathTest` cover persistence and analytics math; graph rendering stays visual.)*

items.name: FIT Export
items.text:
## Steps

items.name: One completed ride carries the whole Strava upload path
items.text:
Nobody would set this up five times. One ride, with Strava linked, tested from the pill before upload to the backlog row after it.

**Setup.** Strava linked, and at least one older session in history that has **not** uploaded — a session recorded before linking is the easiest way to have one. Step 1 reads that session; steps 2 onward use a fresh ride.

## Procedure

1. **The outline pill, before any upload.** On a session with `stravaUploadStatus` unset and Strava linked, the history row shows a white pill with an orange border: `[☁ CloudUpload] Strava`. Tap it — the status flips to `uploading`.
2. **Auto-upload after a completed workout.** Complete a workout. The upload starts on its own, with no tap, and the activity appears on Strava.
3. **The uploading pill.** While either upload is in flight, the pill is the solid-orange `Uploading…` variant with a white spinner.
4. **The activity id reaches the database.** Within about 60 s of upload success — the worker polls — this returns a non-null long: `adb shell "run-as com.yourtrainer sqlite3 databases/your_trainer_database 'SELECT stravaActivityId FROM workout_sessions WHERE sessionId=?'"`. This is the only step that needs a terminal rather than the screen, so it is named on its own.
5. **View on Strava.** With `stravaActivityId` stored, the pill reads `View on Strava`, solid orange. Tap it — `strava.com/activities/{id}` opens in the Strava app, falling back to the browser.
6. **The backlog row disappears once nothing is pending.** With every session now uploaded, the Strava subsection's `Backlog` row is **not rendered at all** — not empty, absent.

## On iOS

Steps 1 to 3, 5 and 6 are tested as written. Step 4 has no terminal query on iOS. Instead, close the app completely, reopen it and open the same ride: its pill still reads `View on Strava`, and tapping it opens the same activity as before. Only a stored activity id survives the relaunch, so this is the iOS evidence for step 4. Edwin chose this evidence on 2026-09-17 ([[ISS-0444-CheckNotesTheV220ProceduresFoundStaleOrUnwalkable]]).

## Expect

- Step 1: the older session shows a white pill with an orange border reading "Strava". Tapping it starts the upload.
- Step 2: the upload starts on its own, with no tap, and the activity appears on Strava.
- Step 3: while uploading, the pill is solid orange and reads "Uploading…" with a white spinner.
- [android] Step 4: the query returns a non-null activity id.
- [ios] Step 4: after the relaunch the pill still reads "View on Strava" and opens the same activity.
- Step 5: the pill reads "View on Strava", solid orange, and opens that activity in Strava or the browser.
- Step 6: the Strava subsection has no Backlog row at all, not an empty one.

## Rows this row absorbed — 2026-09-12

| Retired | What it asked for | Taken at |
| --- | --- | --- |
| [[TST-0472-Upload-Pill-Not-Uploaded-Linked]] | the outline pill, and the tap that starts an upload | steps 1 and 3 |
| [[TST-0473-View-Strava-Pill-Known-Activity-Id]] | the `View on Strava` pill and its deep link | step 5 |
| [[TST-0481-StravaActivityId-Capture-Upload-Happy-Path]] | the `stravaActivityId` column populated after upload | step 4 |
| [[TST-0476-Backlog-Row-Hidden-When-Empty]] | the backlog row absent when nothing is pending | step 6 |

## What one tick no longer distinguishes

- **TST-0472** — the manual tap-to-upload path and the automatic one are different entry points, and a broken tap now hides behind a working auto-upload.
- **TST-0473** — a deep link that opens the wrong activity, or nothing, records as the same failure as an upload that never happened.
- **TST-0481** — this is the only database assertion in the set, and it can fail while every pill on screen looks right; that is why it stays its own numbered step with its query written out.
- **TST-0476** — a backlog row rendered empty is a cosmetic defect sharing a verdict with five functional ones.

## Evidence (fill after running)

- The pill's appearance at each stage, the `adb` query's output, and whether the backlog row was present.

items.name: History tells the ride types apart — by label, by icon, and by filter chip
items.text:
## Setup

A PRO rider. Complete one Zone Ride with a heart-rate strap connected and one Quick Ride before opening History.

Complete a Zone Ride (an HR free ride) and a Quick Ride (a Power free ride), then open History once. Every step below reads off that one screen with those two sessions on it.

**Zone Ride label.** The HR session shows a "Zone Ride" label and a red heart icon.

**Quick Ride label.** The Power session shows a "Quick Ride" label and a purple bolt icon.

**Filter chips present.** The chips All, Power, Route and Heart Rate are visible, each with its label. On Android they are in a row under the **Past Sessions** heading in History. On iOS they are in the History strip, which sits above the bottom bar on a phone and under History in the rail on a tablet.

**Filter chips work.** Tap "Heart Rate" — only the HR session remains. Tap "All" — both come back.

*(partially automated: `WorkoutSessionRepositoryTest.workoutType_persisted_through_insert` covers the POWER / ROUTE / HR_ZONE discriminator round-tripping through the repository; `HistoryTypeFilterRowTest` covers chip rendering and click-to-emit. The labels, the icons and the effect the chips have on a real list stay visual.)*

Two rides is the minimum that makes the filter meaningful, which is why the labels and the filter share a section: with one session on screen a filter proves nothing.

## Expect

- Zone Ride: a "Zone Ride" label and a red heart icon.
- Quick Ride: a "Quick Ride" label and a purple bolt icon.
- The chips All, Power, Route and Heart Rate, each labelled.
- "Heart Rate" leaves only the HR session; "All" brings both back.

## What this row absorbed

- `TST-0191` (History Type Filter) — the filter chips being present and actually narrowing the list. It is the **Filter chips present** and **Filter chips work** steps. Its own note said the chip effect "still requires real session data" — this row is where that data exists.

## What a single tick no longer distinguishes

One tick no longer separates a wrong session label from a filter chip that does nothing. The label is a per-row render and the filter is a list query, so a rider must write down which named step failed.

items.name: History shows the route ride, and the Route filter finds it
items.text:
Complete a Route ride, then open History. One completed ride answers both steps.

## Setup

Any rider with a trainer connected. Complete one Route ride, and have at least one Power session in History to filter out.

## Steps

1. **The session row is labelled.** The row shows a "Route" label and the Route-tab icon (bike / location).
2. **The Route filter chip works.** Tap the "Route" chip. On Android the filters are in a row under the **Past Sessions** heading in History. On iOS they are in the History strip, which sits above the bottom bar on a phone and under History in the rail on a tablet. Only Route sessions remain in the list.

## Expect

- Step 1: the row shows a "Route" label and the Route icon (bike / location).
- Step 2: only Route sessions remain in the list.

## What it absorbed, and what one tick no longer separates

| Absorbed | Step | What a single tick no longer distinguishes |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `TST-0261` | 2 | A filter chip that lets a Power session through now fails the same tick as a session row missing its Route label, though only one of the two involves the filter predicate. |

*(partially automated: `WorkoutSessionRepositoryTest` covers session persistence and the `workoutType` round-trip; `WorkoutHistoryViewModelTest` covers the chip state driving the session predicate. Both renderings stay manual.)*

items.name: Three PB rides — the trophy, the PBs filter, and what happens when the holder is deleted
items.text:
## Setup

A rider with no personal best yet on one workout. Ride that workout three times, each ride beating the one before.

Complete three rides of the same workout, each one beating the previous PB. Open History. The steps run in the order below, because the last one destroys the state the others need.

**Trophy on the latest row.** The first row — the latest ride — shows a trophy icon.

**PBs filter.** Tap the "PBs" chip. On Android the filters are in a row under the **Past Sessions** heading in History. On iOS they are in the History strip, which sits above the bottom bar on a phone and under History in the rail on a tablet. All three rows appear, because each was a PB at save time even though only the last is still the current PB.

**Delete promotes the next best.** Test this last. Delete the ride that holds the current PB. Reopen the library: the PB chip now shows the next-best qualifying attempt's metric, or disappears if no qualifying attempt remains.

*(mostly automated: `PersonalBestServiceTest` covers the `PbState` transitions, the promotion on deleting a PB holder, and the row clearing when the last qualifying attempt goes; `HistoryTypeFilterRowTest.pbs_chip_displayed_alongside_type_chips` and `tapping_pbs_chip_fires_toggle` cover the chip UI and its dispatch. The trophy on real history rows, the filter's effect on a real list, and the delete flow stay manual.)*

## Expect

- The latest row shows a trophy icon.
- The PBs filter shows all three rows.
- After the delete, the PB chip shows the next-best qualifying attempt's metric, or disappears if none remains.

## What this row absorbed

- `TST-0322` (Session Delete Promotes Next-Best PB) — deleting a PB-holding ride and checking that the library chip promotes or clears. It is the **Delete promotes the next best** step. It needed a history with a PB in it, which is exactly what this row's three rides build.

## What a single tick no longer distinguishes

One tick no longer separates a missing trophy from a PBs filter that shows the wrong rows, nor either from a delete that fails to promote the next-best attempt. A rider must write down which named step failed.

**Order matters more than usual here.** The delete step removes one of the three PB rows, so testing it before the **PBs filter** step would leave the filter with two rows to find instead of three. Test the three steps in the order written.

## Why this did not merge into TST-0314

`TST-0321`'s three-ride setup strictly contains `TST-0314`'s two-ride one, so folding `TST-0314` in here would have looked free. It is not. The first-attempt and improved-attempt card copy is the feature `TST-0314` exists to check, and it is checked at session end on the ride itself. The trophy and the filter are a different screen entirely. Merging would put a session-end overlay assertion and a History-screen assertion under one tick, and they fail for unrelated reasons.

items.name: The expanded session in History — training metrics, TSS colour, and the peak-power row
items.text:
Complete a workout, open History, and expand the session. Every step below is one scroll down that expanded card.

**Training metrics.** NP, TSS, IF and VI are shown below the Workout Analysis graph.

**TSS colour.** The TSS colour matches the value shown: green below 150, amber between 150 and 300, red above 300.

**Peak power row.** The 5 s, 30 s, 1 min, 5 min and 20 min peak-power values are shown below the training metrics.

*(partially automated: `AnalyticsMathTest` covers the NP / TSS / IF / VI maths; `WorkoutSessionRepositoryTest` and `MetricRepositoryTest` cover session and metric persistence. The card rendering, the colour and the peak-power row stay visual.)*

## Expect

- NP, TSS, IF and VI show below the Workout Analysis graph.
- The TSS colour matches its value: green below 150, amber from 150 to 300, red above 300.
- The 5 s, 30 s, 1 min, 5 min and 20 min peak powers show below the training metrics.

## What this row absorbed

- `TST-0415` (TSS Color Coding) — the TSS value taking a colour from its band. It is the **TSS colour** step.
- `TST-0416` (Peak Power Row) — the five peak-power durations below the metrics. It is the **Peak power row** step.

## What a single tick no longer distinguishes

One tick no longer separates a missing metric from a wrong TSS colour or a missing peak-power row. All three render on the same expanded card, so a rider must write down which named step was wrong.

**Only one TSS band can be checked per session.** `TST-0415` listed three colours, but a single ride produces a single TSS, so a rider was never going to see green, amber and red in one ride. The step is worded as "the colour matches the value shown" for that reason. Checking the other two bands means riding a session that lands in them, and no row asks for that today.

items.name: Open in Strava pill (unknown activity id)
items.text:
On an uploaded session with no `stravaActivityId` yet, the pill reads `Open in Strava` (same solid orange). Tap opens the athlete training feed instead of a specific ride. *(TASK-0388)*

## Expect

items.name: A failed upload — how it gives up, and the Retry pill that follows
items.text:
The failure has to be manufactured before the pill can be read, so the steps run in this order.

## Procedure

1. **Make it fail, and watch it stop trying.** With an upload in flight and the `Uploading…` pill visible, kill WiFi. Within about 10 minutes — three WorkManager retries with exponential backoff — the pill flips to `Retry`. It must not hang in `Uploading…` forever, which is what ISS-0112 was.
2. **The Retry pill.** With Strava linked and the upload failed, the pill reads `[⚠ Warning] Retry`, white with an orange border.
3. **Retry works.** Reconnect and tap the pill. The upload is re-queued, the pill flips to `Uploading…`, and the upload completes.

## Expect

- Step 1: within about ten minutes the pill flips to `Retry`. It never hangs on `Uploading…`.
- Step 2: the `Retry` pill is white with an orange border and a warning icon.
- Step 3: the pill flips to `Uploading…`, and the upload completes.

## Rows this row absorbed — 2026-09-12

| Retired | What it asked for | Taken at |
| --- | --- | --- |
| [[TST-0482-Upload-Timeout-ISS-0112]] | the WiFi-kill timeout path and the reconnect-and-retry completion | steps 1 and 3 |

## What one tick no longer distinguishes

- **TST-0482** — the timeout is the ISS-0112 regression guard and the pill is a rendering check; they now share a verdict, so a spinner that hangs forever and a pill with the wrong icon are recorded identically.

## Evidence (fill after running)

- How long the pill took to flip after WiFi went down, and whether the retry completed.

2. Upgrade to PRO and verify the export runs, writes a file, and that the file opens with the expected header row and one row per session.
